name: Ruber
lede: Ruber is the Latin word for red, a basic color term so settled in antiquity that it stood for the whole idea of being colored at all, though the vivid pink-red swatch our own library files under the name is only one narrow modern slice of that much older, broader word.

sections.title: One of Latin's two basic colors
sections.body: Pastoureau describes a striking asymmetry in classical Latin color vocabulary [1]. Red has a solid basic term, ruber, backed up by a frequently used doublet, rubeus, plus a rich, varied lexicon of further red words beyond those two [1]. Green gets the same simple treatment, a single word, viridis [1][2]. Blue and yellow get nothing comparable: blue is covered only by a few semantically uncertain terms, caeruleus, caesius, lividus among them, and yellow by several ill-defined words, croceus, flavus, galbinus, with no one term taking clear precedence [1][3]. Pastoureau asks, without fully answering, whether this reflects the Romans' comparative lack of interest in pinning blue and yellow down precisely [2]. Black and white sit in a third pattern of their own: each gets not one but two distinct basic terms, dividing the color by quality rather than shade, matte black (ater) against glossy black (niger), plain white (albus) against pure, brilliant white (candidus) [2][4].

sections.title: When "colored" simply meant "red"
sections.body: The word's reach went further than vocabulary alone. Among the Romans, the two Latin words for "colored" and for "red" itself, coloratus and ruber, were treated as simple synonyms [2][5]. St Clair ties that directly to dyeing history: people likely began dyeing cloth somewhere between the sixth and fourth millennia BC, and almost all of the surviving dyed scraps from that period through the Roman era are some shade of red [5]. Ancient Egyptian mummies were wrapped in linens dyed with hematite red, and Osiris, god of the afterlife, carried the title "lord of the red cloth" [5]. Red's primacy as the dye color most civilizations mastered first very likely runs even further back than Rome itself [2].

sections.title: From a quality to a thing
sections.body: For most of classical Latin, color words worked as adjectives or as abstract nouns describing a quality (rubor, "redness," niger, "blackness") rather than as plain nouns naming a color the way English does now [6]. The grammar color ruber, "the color red," was the usual phrasing, with a nominalized neuter form, rubrum, used less often [6]. That changed over the twelfth century, when vernacular habits pushed Latin color words toward standing on their own as plain nouns, a shift grammarians can date with some precision even though its cause is not fully settled [6]. One further, lower-confidence claim worth naming rather than asserting as fact: some sources connect the river Rubicon's own name to ruber, from the reddish color of its waters, though this etymology is not universally accepted [1].

sections.title: A word still working, centuries later
sections.body: The word outlived the empire as working vocabulary, not just a dictionary entry. Linnaeus, building his eighteenth-century system for classifying plants, used a restricted set of only nine basic color terms, and ruber was one of them, alongside albus, niger, luteus, purpureus, caeruleus and viridis [7]. The word surfaces today in a much smaller, more technical register: the Scarlet Ibis carries the scientific name *Eudocimus ruber*, the old Latin word for red sitting quietly inside a modern taxonomic name [8].

sections.title: This swatch is one narrow slice of a very old word
sections.body: What our own library files under "Ruber" is not the ancient word's whole range; it is one specific, vivid pink-leaning red, measured from the xkcd color survey and cross-referenced to ISCC-NBS 1955 block 11, "vivid red" [9]. In the color graph, this exact swatch sits 3.2 units from [[telemagenta]], more vivid, and 3.8 from [[berry-pink]], duller [9]. [[razzmatazz]], 4.7 off, is more vivid again; [[deep-cerise]], 5.2 off, is purpler and more vivid; [[france-rose]], also 5.2 off, is duller; [[red-purple]], 5.4 off, is more vivid [9]. The ancient word covered the whole family of reds; this one modern measurement covers only this one corner of it.

sections.title: Seen in
sections.body: Its two nearest gem twins are Spinel, 5.1 units off, and Ruby, 6.6 off — a fitting pair for a word whose own root sense is simply "red" [10]. On screen, *Blade Runner*'s saturated neon palette lands 4.5 units away, and *Barbie* sits 6.6 off [11]. Pantone's 2001 Color of the Year, Fuchsia Rose, is remarkably close, just 1.9 units off, with 2011's Honeysuckle a touch further at 5.0 [12]. Among design aesthetics, Fauvism is the nearest full-palette match, 2.4 units off on its neighbor Darkish Pink, with McBling and Decora close behind at 2.7 and 3.2, both on this swatch directly [13].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this exact vivid pink-red in only 3 of 23,778 paintings, about 0.01 percent as photographed, with the within-painting lens finding it in just 1 [14]. That makes it rarer than 88 percent of the named colors we measure [14]. The small number is itself informative, not a failure of the method: a narrow, highly saturated pink-red is simply uncommon in painted pigment across most periods and schools, whatever the Latin word's own much broader historical range once covered [14]. In printed English, the word's adjective sense in this color context peaks in the 1970s and rose fastest in the same decade, a far more recent curve than the word's own classical age would suggest [14]. This is a computed color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test.

questions.q: In classical Latin, what did the word "coloratus" ("colored") and "ruber" ("red") have in common?
choices: Coloratus was a brand name for a dye

questions.q: Why did Latin have only one stable basic word for red and green, but none for blue and yellow?
choices: The sources leave this an open question, possibly reflecting less interest in distinguishing those shades precisely
Blue and yellow pigments did not exist in ancient Rome
Roman law forbade naming blue and yellow
Blue and yellow are modern colors invented after Rome
questions.answer: The sources leave this an open question, possibly reflecting less interest in distinguishing those shades precisely

questions.q: Is the ColorHub swatch filed under "Ruber" the same as the full range the ancient Latin word covered?
choices: No, it is one narrow, vivid pink-red measurement, far narrower than the word's historical range
No, because the word never meant red at all
Yes, because Latin had no other red words
questions.answer: No, it is one narrow, vivid pink-red measurement, far narrower than the word's historical range

openers: In classical Latin, the words for "red" and "colored" were simple synonyms — red was the default meaning of color itself.
The ancient word ruber still hides inside a modern scientific name: the Scarlet Ibis, Eudocimus ruber.

issues: Depth wave pilot: built from color-kb concordance (16 hits: Pastoureau's Red/Blue/Yellow/White/Black, St Clair, Baty) plus existing fact cards. Explicitly separates the ancient Latin word's broad historical range from the one narrow, modern xkcd-survey swatch our library files under the same name, to avoid implying they are the same thing. The Rubicon etymology is flagged as lower-confidence rather than asserted outright.
